title: The pilgrim (Ignatius, Autobiography)
hookLine: he calls himself the pilgrim in his own life story
tomorrow: what did a bishop write to people who kept failing?

cards: When a star athlete talks about himself in the third person, the clip goes around and everybody groans. He wants the ball. He isn't worried.
It sounds like ego. Now here's an odd old book. A former soldier tells his life story, years later, to a younger companion who writes it down.
And the storyteller almost never says I. He's he, all the way through, and over and over he's simply the pilgrim. This is Ignatius of Loyola.
So why would a man tell his own story like that?

teach.b: Start where his story starts. A cannonball shatters his leg in the siege of Pamplona. Laid up, he asks for the knight stories he loves.
There are none in the house, so he's handed a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives. Then the noticing.
He catches himself in two kinds of daydreams: winning glory and a great lady's favor, or going barefoot to Jerusalem like the saints. The first kind delight him while they last and leave him dry.
The second leave him content long after. The story calls this noticing the first time he reasoned about the things of God. Then the road.
Once he can walk, he goes to the shrine of Montserrat, leaves his sword at Our Lady's altar, and gives his fine clothes to a poor man.
From here on, he's the pilgrim. Now the answer to the puzzle. The athlete's he is about a star who has arrived.
Ignatius's he is about someone who hasn't.
A pilgrim is on the way, still learning. At Manresa, he says, God treated him the way a schoolteacher treats a child.
Calling himself the pilgrim keeps the story honest: not a hero telling his legend, but a student telling how he was taught.

how: Jesuits and people who make the Spiritual Exercises read Ignatius's own story of his conversion, and Ignatian prayer includes noticing which thoughts leave a person consoled and which leave them dry.

o: a tourist who visits well-known churches
someone on the way, not yet arrived
a monk who never leaves his monastery

games.q: the pilgrim's road — tap the pairs.
p: a life of Christ, the saints' lives
taught like a child at school

s: Ignatius tells his life story mostly as I
he's he, and often the pilgrim, all the way through.
his turn began with books he never asked for
he wanted knight stories; the house had a life of Christ and saints' lives.
talking about yourself as he is always ego
for Ignatius it works the other way: the pilgrim is someone who hasn't arrived.

games.q: your cousin writes his college essay like a highlight reel: every win, no lessons. by Ignatius's way of telling a life, what's missing?
o: the road: where he was still learning, and what taught him.
more wins, told as he instead of I so it sounds humble.
nothing; a life story should show you've already arrived.
games.why: Ignatius tells his life as the pilgrim, a man still on the way, taught by God the way a schoolteacher teaches a child.

practice: Say yesterday out loud, softly, in Ignatius's style and without the word I: the pilgrim woke up late, the pilgrim was kind to someone, or wasn't. Notice which moments left you dry and which left you content.
If you pray, you can hand the pilgrim's day to God.

wordCard.voice: The pilgrim. The name Ignatius gives himself in his own story: someone on the way, still being taught. Today's word.

orig.note: Spanish for pilgrim (Latin peregrinus): the name Ignatius gives himself.

carryVoice: The line to keep: the pilgrim, not a legend but a student on the road. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Autobiography (Reminiscences), §§1–8 (the wound, the books, the two kinds of thoughts)
